builder_plan.scenario: A workflow needs specialist review, but extra agents may add more cost than useful work.
builder_plan.change: Test the proposed division of work against a single-agent implementation.
builder_plan.baseline: One agent with the same tools and an equal total token and time budget.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Accepted outputs, coordination failures, wall-clock time, and total cost across all agents.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Create Your Own Work Stack: Deploying Self-hosted AI and Tooling in a Tech Startup
summary: The method replaces routing all development and coordination tasks to commercial AI agents with a hybrid stack where commercial models handle complex coding while self-hosted local models handle lower-complexity tasks, documentation synchronization, and retrieval from tools such as Outline, Plane, and ERPNext. It costs self-hosting infrastructure and integration effort, accepts that local models are insufficiently capable and fast for complex coding, and adds task-routing complexity; commercial cost savings are estimated rather than directly measured. Adoption can fail from UX friction if deployment is not centrally configured, and the savings depend entirely on whether a workload actually contains a large fraction of low-complexity coordination tasks.
rationale: The hybrid routing pattern is feasible on constrained infrastructure and matches the reader's cost-control goal, but the reported savings are self-reported estimates tied to one company's workflow, so the reader must validate the coordination-task fraction in their own workload before adopting.

claims.statement: The method replaces routing all development and coordination tasks to commercial AI agents with a hybrid stack where commercial models handle complex coding while self-hosted local models handle lower-complexity tasks, documentation synchronization, and retrieval from tools such as Outline, Plane, and ERPNext. It costs self-hosting infrastructure and integration effort, accepts that local models are insufficiently capable and fast for complex coding, and adds task-routing complexity; commercial cost savings are estimated rather than directly measured. Adoption can fail from UX friction if deployment is not centrally configured, and the savings depend entirely on whether a workload actually contains a large fraction of low-complexity coordination tasks.

The paper estimates that 30--40% of commercial-AI workload is operational coordination, of which about 90% can be moved to local models, corresponding to an estimated 27--36% reduction in overall commercial-AI workload or cost-equivalent usage (approximately 1.37x cost reduction).
